content: Gac, scientifically known as Momordica cochinchinensis (Lour.), is a fruit native to Southeast Asia, spanning regions from Southern China to Northeastern Australia. It is commonly referred to as baby jackfruit, spiny bitter gourd, sweet gourd, or cochinchin gourd. In Vietnamese, it is called gấc or quả gấc, and in Chinese, it is known as 木鳖果. This fruit has been traditionally utilized both as a food source and for medicinal purposes in the areas where it naturally grows. The fruit has a relatively short harvest season, peaking in December and January, which makes it less abundant compared to other foods. Due to its limited availability, gac is often reserved for ceremonial or festive occasions in Vietnam, such as Tết (the Vietnamese New Year) and weddings. A popular dish prepared with gac is xôi gấc, where the aril and seeds of the fruit are cooked with glutinous rice, imparting a vibrant color and unique flavor to the dish. In recent years, gac has gained attention outside of Asia, particularly in the form of juice and dietary supplements, due to its purportedly high phytonutrient content. The fruit grows on dioecious vines, which are often cultivated on fences or lattices, especially in rural areas. These vines typically bear fruit only once a year, and the fruit is seasonally available in local markets. When ripe, the fruit turns a dark orange color and is usually round or oblong, measuring approximately 13 cm in length and 10 cm in diameter. Its exterior is covered in small spines, while the interior contains clusters of dark red, fleshy pulp and seeds. Beyond its culinary uses, gac is valued for its medicinal and nutritional properties. In Vietnam, the seed membranes are traditionally used to alleviate dry eyes and promote healthy vision. Similarly, in Traditional Chinese Medicine, the seeds, known as mubiezi (木鳖子), are employed for various internal and external therapeutic purposes. Recent chemical analyses of gac have revealed its exceptionally high concentrations of important phytonutrients. Notably, it contains up to 70 times more lycopene per unit mass than tomatoes and up to 10 times more beta-carotene than carrots or sweet potatoes. Furthermore, the carotenoids in gac are bound to long-chain fatty acids, which are believed to enhance their bioavailability. Emerging research also suggests that gac contains a protein that may inhibit the proliferation of cancer cells, highlighting its potential as a functional food with significant health benefits.
